rules.title: 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement AI terms
rules.applies_when: a SAG-AFTRA-covered film/TV/streaming production scans performers or background actors, makes or uses digital replicas (including from the picture's own footage), digitally alters performances, dubs with a replica, uses a generative-AI 'Synthetic' in a human role, or licenses covered performances for AI training
requires: Treat a replica built from the picture's own photography, without a scan, as an employment-based digital replica with all protections (39A).
Judge whether an alteration needs new consent against only the script given to the performer on or before the last day they performed the scene (39B).
Pay at least the day performer rate for an independently created replica, plus residuals where a natural performer would earn them; consent and benefit contributions still apply (39C).
Get the performer's consent before using a replica to dub their performance into another language, for pictures starting principal photography on or after 2027-07-01 (39D).
Do not use performers' or background actors' fingerprints, palmprints or iris scans for purposes unrelated to the picture, other than set security systems (39E).
Never use a minor's replica to depict the minor nude or in simulated sexual activity, including by ageing up or de-ageing (39F, 43E).
Do not use a replica during a strike where consent is required and the performer could refuse to work (39G).
Limit access to replicas to people with a legitimate business need and use commercially reasonable efforts against unauthorized access, use or copying (39H).

If transferring ownership of a replica, the producer stays responsible unless the union approves the transferee's financial responsibility and the transferee agrees in writing to comply; the union answers within 21 days (39I).
Have an articulable business reason when asking a performer or background actor to consent to a scan; it need not be disclosed automatically (39J).

Give notice and bargain before using a Synthetic (a generative-AI asset that reads as a natural performer but is not recognizable as or voiced by one); do not use one in a human role unless it brings 'significant additional value', including compared with a digital replica (39K).
Notify the union in writing, and meet on request, if licensing covered performances for compensation to a non-affiliated third party to train a public-facing commercial generative AI system (39L).
Use interview or audition recordings (including self-tapes) only for casting, and do not make them public without the performer's written consent obtained at the time of use (7C).
evidence: Scan-request record with the stated business reason, consent, and the performer's or background actor's identity
Replica asset register: source footage or scan, creation date, holder, people with access, access log, and security measures
Transfer record for any replica that changes hands, with union approval and the transferee's written undertaking
Consent records tied to each replica use, including dubbing consents for pictures starting principal photography on or after 2027-07-01
The script version (and date given to the performer) used to judge whether an alteration was within what was scripted
Flag on any replica or shot involving a minor, with confirmation that no nude or sexual depiction (including age-shifting) was generated
Synthetic-use file: union notice, bargaining record, and the 'significant additional value' justification per role
Record that biometric identifiers were not used outside the picture
Union notice and license record for any sale of performance data for AI training
workflow_signals: photogrammetry, Gaussian-splat or volumetric capture of performers or background actors
identity LoRAs, face embeddings or voice models built from the picture's own footage (a 'no scan' replica)
replica assets stored, copied or handed to another vendor
lip-sync or voice-conversion nodes producing another language
age-shifting (de-ageing or ageing up) nodes on any performer, especially a minor
photoreal synthetic human characters in speaking or featured roles
dataset export or training on production footage for a third party
rules.human_in_loop: Indirect: the synthetic-performer standard favors human performance, so keep records of which roles humans performed.

rules.authority: U.S. Copyright Office
rules.title: Copyright and AI, Part 2: Copyrightability
rules.status: guidance
rules.applies_when: a studio wants copyright protection in content that contains AI-generated material
requires: Only human authorship is protected. Purely AI-generated material is not protected, and neither is material where the human lacked sufficient control over the expressive elements.
Prompts alone, including repeatedly revised prompts, do not currently give enough control to make the user an author.
Human expressive inputs that remain perceptible in the output (e.g. an artist's own drawing, plate or model) stay protected.
Creative selection, coordination, arrangement or modification of AI output can be protected, case by case.
AI used to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect protection of the human work. Commenters' examples include de-aging actors and removing unwanted objects or crowds.

A larger human-authored work that includes AI-generated elements stays protected as a whole. The report's example is a film with AI-generated special effects or background art, where the AI elements are not protected on their own.
No new legislation or sui generis right is recommended.
evidence: Human-made inputs per shot: plates, paintovers, 3D layouts, sketches, control maps, with author IDs
Record of human modifications after generation (comp, paint, roto, grading) with before/after versions
Selection and arrangement decisions (which takes were chosen and why, the edit)
Prompt and seed history, which shows process but is not by itself evidence of authorship
workflow_signals: ControlNet/depth/pose/img2img nodes driven by human-made inputs
pure text-to-image/video with no human input image
post-generation comp/paint steps in Nuke or similar
rules.human_in_loop: Central. Protection depends on the human's expressive contribution, so the workflow history should separate human inputs and edits from model output.
rules.source_title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
rules.notes: This is agency guidance; courts decide case by case. The Office said it would issue further registration guidance and update the Compendium, but copyright.gov/ai lists no such update as of 2026-10-15. Part 3 (training) still exists only as the 2025-05-09 pre-publication version (see usco-part3-generative-ai-training). The Register's May 2025 removal has not taken effect: the D.C. Circuit enjoined it pending appeal (Sept. 2025), the Supreme Court denied the government's stay application on 2026-06-30, and the district-court suit is stayed to 2026-12-18 while H.R. 6028 is pending in the Senate. Allen v. Perlmutter (D. Colo. 1:24-cv-2665) tests the Part 2 approach on a heavily iterated Midjourney image; no ruling was reported as of 2026-10-15 (see allen-v-perlmutter).

rules.title: AI Act Art. 50(2): machine-readable marking of synthetic output
rules.status: applies from 2026-08-02 (the AI Act itself has been in force since 2024-08-01); providers of generative systems placed on the market before 2026-08-02 must comply by 2026-12-02 (Art. 111(4), added by the Digital Omnibus, Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)
rules.applies_when: the studio is a provider of a generative AI system whose synthetic audio, image, video or text output is used in the EU. Under the Commission's Art. 50 guidelines, a company is a provider if it develops a generative system (or has one developed) and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name, including for its own in-house use. A company that modifies an existing generative system (e.g. with new training data) and puts it into service under its own name also becomes a provider. Free and open-source model components that are not themselves an AI system are outside Art. 50, but open-source AI systems are not exempt.
requires: Mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they are detectable as AI-generated or manipulated, and make a means of detection available.
Marking must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, considering content type, cost, the state of the art and technical standards.

Exempt: AI performing an assistive function for standard editing, or not substantially altering the input or its meaning. The guidelines' examples of exempt edits include colour correction, noise reduction, rescaling, stabilisation, dust or red-eye removal and aspect-ratio pixel filling. Examples that need marking include face replacement, object or person insertion/removal that changes meaning, realistic synthetic speech in a specific person's voice, and composites that change how persons or events are represented.

Outputs used only in closed-loop industrial or product-development workflows (the guidelines name film, animation, games and advertising production) need not be marked unless they are the final output; only the final output of the workflow has to be marked and detectable.
A company that builds an in-house generative system and uses it to make deepfakes is both a provider (Art. 50(2) marking) and a deployer (Art. 50(4) labelling).
evidence: Whether the studio acts as a provider (own or modified generative system put into service under its name, including in-house) or only as a deployer of third-party tools, with the reasoning
Per output: whether it is a final deliverable or a closed-loop intermediate inside the production pipeline
Per AI operation: classification as standard editing (exempt) or substantive alteration (marking required), referencing the guidelines' examples
Marking method applied per final output (signed metadata / C2PA manifest, watermark), and verification that it survives the delivery pipeline
Vendor contract terms guaranteeing marking by upstream system providers
workflow_signals: studio-trained or fine-tuned models/LoRAs offered as a service or tool

metadata-stripping steps (re-encode, EXR/ProRes conversion) that could remove marks
rules.human_in_loop: None. Art. 50 is about marking and disclosure, not human oversight.

rules.title: AI Act Art. 50(4): deepfake disclosure by deployers
rules.status: applies from 2026-08-02 (no transitional period for deployers; content generated before 2026-08-02 need not be labelled retroactively, per the Commission Q&A)
rules.applies_when: a studio, under its own authority, uses an AI system to generate or manipulate image, audio or video that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic (a deepfake, Art. 3(60)), and the content is used in the EU. A deployer established outside the EU is covered where it directs or authorises distribution in the EU (including posting on the globally accessible internet), but not where content reaches the EU through unforeseeable channels outside its control. A client that merely commissions content without deciding or controlling whether and how AI is used is not a deployer; the vendor that does decide is.
requires: Disclose that deepfake content is artificially generated or manipulated, clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at first exposure, and accessibly. A visible or audible label is needed; the provider's machine-readable marking does not satisfy this duty.

For deepfakes in evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works or programmes, the duty is limited to disclosure in an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work. What is appropriate is a case-by-case assessment.

'Evidently' is read strictly: if the creative nature is unclear to the audience, the lighter regime does not apply. Where content mixes informative and creative character, the informative character prevails. Advertising and documentaries qualify only in specific situations.

The guidelines say AI-generated background scenes, special effects and standard pre- and post-processing in movie production are unlikely to be deepfakes. Fully AI-generated actors, digital replicas of real or deceased actors, de-aging and simulated performances are likely to be deepfakes, though a film featuring them in a cinema or on streaming is an example of an evidently artistic/fictional work.
Fantastical content (e.g. a sphinx flying over the Eiffel Tower) and fictional characters' AI voices without deception as to identity are not deepfakes.
Disclosure at the start of the content may be insufficient if audiences foreseeably join later; complement it with later disclosure where possible.
The lighter regime does not excuse infringing third parties' rights (personal data, intellectual property).
evidence: Per-deliverable flag: contains a realistic AI-generated or manipulated depiction of real-seeming persons, places or events (Y/N), with the reasoning (VFX/background vs. digital replica, de-aging, synthetic performer)

requires: A work is protected only if it is the author's own intellectual creation, reflecting their personality through free and creative choices (Painer: for portrait photos, choices such as framing, angle, lighting and setting).
Choices dictated by technical constraints or function that leave no room for creativity do not qualify (Football Dataco, per commentary). A free choice is not automatically a creative one.

The creative choices must be identifiable with precision and objectivity in the subject matter; aesthetic effect alone is not enough, and there is no higher threshold for applied art (Mio/konektra, 4 Dec 2025).
Infringement asks whether protectable creative elements of the original are recognisably taken over, not whether the overall impression is similar (Mio/konektra).

requires: For a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work that is computer-generated, the author is taken to be the person who made the arrangements necessary for its creation (s9(3)).

rules.authority: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA); IPTC (digital source type vocabulary)
rules.title: C2PA Content Credentials + IPTC digital source types
rules.status: voluntary standard; current version 2.4 (April 2026)
rules.applies_when: a studio wants machine-readable provenance on deliverables (supports Art. 50, SB 942, China implicit labels, and platform auto-labelling)
requires: A manifest is a signed claim bundling assertions (actions, ingredients, metadata, thumbnails, content bindings); the manifests together form the asset's Content Credentials.

Every standard manifest must contain exactly one c2pa.created or c2pa.opened action, and it must be the first action in the first actions assertion. Update manifests follow different rules. Ingredients (source assets) are linked by reference; from 2.4 a c2pa.opened action must carry a hashed-URI reference to its ingredient assertion.
Actions can carry a digitalSourceType from the IPTC vocabulary. Spec 2.4 also allows an ingredient without its own manifest to carry a digitalSourceType.

Spec 2.4 adds an optional AI Disclosure assertion (c2pa.ai-disclosure). It records the model type (required), and optionally the model name and identifier (e.g. a PURL) and a humanOversightLevel of fully_autonomous, prompt_guided or human_validated. It is meant to complement, not replace, actions and digitalSourceType.

IPTC codes most relevant to VFX: trainedAlgorithmicMedia (created with GenAI, e.g. text-to-image or text-to-video); compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia (an existing capture edited with GenAI, e.g. inpainting, outpainting, GenAI effects on camera footage); compositeSynthetic (a mix of elements, at least one of which is GenAI, e.g. live action combined with generated elements); compositeCapture (all captured elements); digitalCapture (camera plates); algorithmicallyEnhanced (non-generative algorithmic fixes such as sharpening or denoising); digitalCreation (human-made with non-generative tools).
Soft bindings (watermarks or fingerprints) can help recover provenance after metadata is stripped.
evidence: Signed manifest per deliverable listing ingredients (plates, generated elements), actions and digitalSourceType
Where used: a c2pa.ai-disclosure assertion naming the model(s) and the human oversight level

rules.authority: European Commission
rules.title: Commission Guidelines on AI Act Art. 50 transparency, C(2026) 5054: film and VFX treatment
rules.status: adopted 2026-07-20; non-binding interpretive guidance (CJEU has final say)
rules.applies_when: a studio produces AI-assisted image, video or audio for distribution in the EU and needs to decide whether outputs must be machine-marked (Art. 50(2)) or labelled as deepfakes (Art. 50(4))
requires: Intermediate outputs used only inside closed-loop film, animation, games or advertising production need not be marked; only the final output must be (para. 68).

Standard edits are exempt from marking (e.g. colour correction, noise reduction, rescaling, stabilisation, aspect-ratio pixel filling); face replacement, meaning-changing object/person insertion or removal, and realistic voice synthesis of a specific person are not (para. 92).

AI backgrounds, special effects and standard pre/post-processing in movie production are unlikely to be deepfakes; AI actors, digital replicas, de-aging and simulated performances are likely to be (para. 114).

Films and trailers with such deepfakes, shown in cinemas or on streaming, are an example of evidently artistic/fictional works, so a non-intrusive disclosure suffices; the deployer still has to disclose (paras 119-124).
Product ads using AI imagery that could mislead about the product, or synthetic people demonstrating products, do not benefit from the artistic regime (paras 114, 124 examples).
Deployers outside the EU are covered when they direct or authorise EU distribution; a client that does not control AI use is not a deployer (paras 13-14).

Per deliverable: deepfake assessment (VFX/background vs. replica, de-aging, synthetic performer), and whether the artistic/fictional regime is relied on

Which party (studio, vendor, client) decided and controlled the AI use

Provider publishes a sufficiently detailed summary of training content using the AI Office template (published 2025-07-24) (Art. 53(1)(d)).

Open-weight models under a free and open-source licence (no monetisation, weights and architecture public) are exempt only from (a) and (b); the copyright policy and the training-data summary still apply, and models with systemic risk get no exemption (Art. 53(2)).
Providers may show compliance through the GPAI Code of Practice (Art. 53(4)).

Written approval is reported as required for: Netflix proprietary data or personal information in tools; third-party material from artists, performers or other rights holders; GenAI key story elements (main characters, key visuals, fictional settings); prompts referencing copyrighted works, public figures or deceased people; significant digital alteration of performances (e.g. visual ADR); and GenAI material in final deliverables.
Digital replicas or meaningful changes to a performance need the performer's consent. Coverage reports routine post work (cosmetic touch-ups, noise reduction, timing fixes) as lower risk.
Vendors' custom GenAI workflows must meet the same principles at every step.

rules.authority: Motion Picture Association / Trusted Partner Network (TPN), MPA subsidiary
rules.title: MPA Content Security Best Practices v5.3.2: AI Supplemental v1.0 (AI/ML controls)
rules.status: current version; v5.3.2 with AI Supplemental v1.0 dated 2026-09-23. The document calls these minimum security expectations of most MPA member studios; they are enforced through TPN assessments and client contracts, not law.
rules.applies_when: a vendor handles content of MPA member studios (Netflix, Paramount, Amazon, Sony Pictures, Universal, Disney, Warner Bros.) or is TPN-assessed, and uses AI/ML tools on client content
requires: Keep an AI/ML security-management policy that covers client inputs, prompts, outputs, embeddings, fine-tuned weights or adapters, caches, logs and other artifacts derived from client content; obtain client approval for AI/ML application use (OR-5.0).
Keep an inventory of approved content-handling AI tools, scripts, services and APIs (e.g. an AI SBOM), and identify and manage 'shadow' AI use (TS-7.2).
Get written client approval before applying any AI tool or service to client content, keep approval records per project, and tell clients about AI tool use on request (TS-7.2).
Keep an audit log of AI actions: prompts, guardrails, actions taken, systems accessed, workflow stage, outputs produced, account identity and timestamp (TS-7.2).
Classify system prompts and AI configuration at the same sensitivity as the client content they process (TS-7.2).
Flow AI governance requirements down to subcontractors; notify clients of suspected AI incidents affecting content within 24 hours (TS-7.2).

Scan pre-trained models, datasets and models from public repositories before use, and import pre-trained LLMs into a segmented, restricted network first. Get written client consent before using content to train or fine-tune models (TS-7.0).

For third-party AI services, confirm the provider cannot use client content for training or other purposes beyond the project, prefer zero or least retention, and confirm cross-client isolation (TS-7.4).

For in-house AI, keep an SBOM of models, libraries and APIs (version, source, intended use, approval status), and recommended: track training datasets' origin and approvals and verify model artifacts cryptographically, e.g. by checksum (TS-7.3).
For agentic AI, a human must approve material actions beforehand; notification after the action is not approval (TS-7.5).
Recommended (not a baseline control): where the client requires it, track content integrity consistent with C2PA or equivalent (TS-7.2 additional recommendation).
Separate content and production networks from the internet and office networks by physical air gap or logical VLAN segmentation, with no dual-homed bridging (TS-2.5).
evidence: Per-project written client approval of each AI tool or service used on client content
Approved AI tool inventory/SBOM entry for every node pack, model, LoRA and API used, with version, source and approval status
Per-run AI audit log: prompt, model, workflow stage, outputs, operator account, timestamp
Model scan record and checksum for each downloaded model before it entered the content network
Data-handling terms for any third-party AI API (no training, retention period, tenant isolation)
Written client consent if client content was used to train or fine-tune (e.g. a LoRA trained on plates)
Optional: C2PA manifest for deliverables where the client requires it
workflow_signals: every model or LoRA loader (needs inventory, scan and checksum)
API or partner nodes that send client content off-premises
training or fine-tuning on client plates (LoRA training)
LLM or agent nodes acting on files
nodes or custom packs that fetch from the internet on a content network

rules.title: UK advertising codes applied to AI-generated content (no blanket AI label)
rules.status: in force (CAP/BCAP Codes; guidance articles May 2025 and June 2026)
rules.applies_when: an ad within ASA remit (non-broadcast under CAP, TV/radio under BCAP) contains AI-generated or AI-altered imagery, voices or people
requires: There is no blanket requirement to disclose AI use in UK ads. Existing CAP and BCAP rules apply however the content was made.

A disclosure cannot fix a fundamentally misleading ad, e.g. an AI image that overstates a product's results.
A realistic AI 'endorsement' by a celebrity that could mislead likely breaches the Code. Using a public figure's likeness raises separate personality and IP rights issues.
Check AI outputs for harmful stereotypes and social responsibility. The advertiser remains responsible even when tools or platforms automate production.
evidence: Record of whether the ad contains AI-generated people, voices or product depictions, and the disclosure decision with rationale
Substantiation that product depictions are not exaggerated by AI (e.g. untouched reference footage)

Human review sign-off for bias and social responsibility

celebrity or public-figure likeness

rules.authority: California Legislature (SB 1050, Chapter 246 of 2026; Bus. & Prof. Code s17610)
rules.title: SB 1050: synthetic performer disclosure in advertising
rules.status: signed 2026-09-16; operative 2027-01-01

requires: Include a clear and conspicuous disclosure with wording substantially similar to 'This performance features a synthetic performer' or 'No human performer is depicted'.
'Prominently' covers synthetic performers in the foreground demonstrating a product, narrating, or illustrating or reacting to the message.
No knowledge requirement, and audio-only ads are covered (unlike New York).
Exempt: ads for expressive works (film, TV, streaming, documentaries, games) where the synthetic performer is used consistently with the work; AI used only for language translation.
Violations are treated as false advertising (B&P s17500) and enforceable under the Unfair Competition Law, including potentially by private plaintiffs.

The exact disclosure wording and its placement on each California deliverable

rules.title: Living-person right of publicity covers digital replicas

requires: Obtain consent before using a living person's voice or likeness, including a digital replica, on or in products or for advertising.
Remedies include statutory damages of $750 or actual damages plus attributable profits, punitive damages and fees; SB 683 added injunctions and TROs with removal within two business days of service.

SB 1111 also treats use of a digital replica with intent to impersonate as false impersonation under the Penal Code, and removes the rebuttable presumption covering incidental use of an employee's likeness in ads.
Exempt: news, public affairs, sports and political campaigns; ad media are liable only with knowledge.
evidence: Signed consent or licence for any living person's voice or likeness used in ads or merchandise, including AI replicas
For employee likeness in marketing, a signed release (the presumption no longer applies after 2027-01-01)

rules.authority: Illinois General Assembly (Right of Publicity Act, 765 ILCS 1075, as amended by HB 4875, Public Act 103-0836)
rules.title: Illinois Right of Publicity Act: unauthorized digital replicas
rules.status: in force
rules.applies_when: a sound recording or audiovisual work containing a digital replica of a real individual's voice, image or likeness (made with AI or other technology, in a work the person did not perform in) is distributed or made available to the public
requires: Do not knowingly distribute, transmit or make available a sound recording or audiovisual work with actual knowledge that it contains an unauthorized digital replica (one made without consent of the rights holder).
Post-mortem: for deaths after 2025-01-01, commercial use of identity or a digital replica needs consent for 50 years after death.
Anyone who knowingly facilitates such distribution after gaining actual knowledge can also be liable.

Unlike the general film/TV exemption (which covers only the commercial-use and post-mortem rules), replica exemptions are narrower: news and political uses; newsworthy uses, documentaries, docudramas and biographical works unless they create a false impression of an authentic recording or participation; comment, criticism, satire, parody; ads for those uses.
evidence: Consent from the depicted individual or rights holder for every real-person replica in a released work
For documentary or biographical uses: note why the replica does not create a false impression of authentic participation

rules.title: Canada: copyright in AI-assisted works requires a human author exercising skill and judgment
rules.status: current law (no AI-specific ruling; CIPPIC v Sahni pending)
rules.applies_when: a studio claims or relies on Canadian copyright in a shot or work that contains AI-generated material
requires: Existing case law indicates authorship must be attributed to a human who exercises skill and judgment; no Canadian court has yet ruled on AI authorship.

Names of the human authors per work

rules.authority: Copyright Act Art. 30-4; Agency for Cultural Affairs (Legal Subcommittee, Copyright Subdivision of the Cultural Council)
rules.title: Japan: AI training under Art. 30-4 and its limits
rules.status: in force (statute); guidance published 2024
rules.applies_when: a studio or vendor trains, fine-tunes (e.g. LoRA) or builds RAG over copyrighted works in Japan
requires: Training for data analysis without a purpose of 'enjoying' the works is generally allowed without permission.

Art. 30-4 does not apply where an enjoyment purpose coexists, e.g. fine-tuning or intentional overfitting on a small set of one creator's works to output their creative expression, or RAG designed to output inputted expression.
The proviso excludes uses that unreasonably prejudice the owner, such as copying a licensable analysis database while circumventing technical measures like robots.txt or access controls.
Knowingly collecting training data from pirate sites raises the risk of liability for infringing outputs.
evidence: Dataset manifest for any studio-trained or fine-tuned model (sources, licences, whether a single creator's work dominates)
Record of crawler compliance with robots.txt and access controls
workflow_signals: LoRA or fine-tune trained on a single artist's or studio's works
RAG or reference-image pipelines that reproduce source expression

rules.notes: The General Understanding is not legally binding; it is the subcommittee's interpretation of current law. rules.authority: Agency for Cultural Affairs (Legal Subcommittee, Copyright Subdivision of the Cultural Council)
rules.title: Japan: infringement by AI outputs and copyrightability of AI-assisted works
rules.status: published (non-binding interpretation)
rules.applies_when: AI-generated material is used, published or sold in Japan, or a studio claims Japanese copyright in it
requires: Outputs infringe on the ordinary test: similarity of creative expression plus reliance on the existing work.
Reliance is generally presumed if the work was in the model's training data, even if the user did not know it; it can also be inferred from user access or high similarity.
A style alone is an idea and is not protected, but outputs reproducing common creative expression of a creator's body of work can infringe.

Purely autonomous output (no instruction or a simple prompt) is not a work; AI used as a tool with creative intention and creative contribution can be, judged case by case: detailed expressive instructions, iterative correction while checking outputs, some creative selection, and human additions or edits.
Both users and AI businesses can be liable; remedies can include injunctions, destruction of outputs and, in some cases, dataset removal.
evidence: Similarity check against known reference works for hero assets
Prompt, iteration and edit history showing human creative contribution
Record of models used and their training-data disclosures
workflow_signals: prompts naming artists or titles
img2img or reference-driven generation from third-party works
iterative refinement and manual paint-over
rules.human_in_loop: Yes for protectability: Japan weighs creative intention and contribution, so the iteration and edit history matters.
rules.source_title: General Understanding on AI and Copyright in Japan - Overview (Japan Copyright Office, Agency for Cultural Affairs)

metadata-stripping export steps

rules.authority: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and Korea Copyright Commission
rules.title: Korea: Guide to Copyright Registration for Generative AI-Assisted Works
rules.status: published
rules.applies_when: a studio registers or relies on Korean copyright in a work containing generative AI output
requires: Purely autonomous AI output is not registrable; a work made with GenAI as a tool is registrable for the parts showing human creative contribution.
Prompting alone is unlikely to count as creative contribution; human modification, selection and arrangement, inpainting, human sketches or a human work used as input can count.
Minor changes (typo fixes, resizing, simple colour changes) do not count; compositing two AI images with simple retouching was refused registration (KCC 2024).
Applications must identify AI-generated and human-created portions separately; only the human portion benefits from registration. The Commission does not examine the degree of human contribution.

Documentation of the creation process (the guide suggests e.g. screen recordings)
workflow_signals: any final deliverable containing generative output that the studio intends to register in Korea
inpainting and manual compositing steps

rules.authority: IATSE / AMPTP
rules.title: 2024 IATSE Basic Agreement: Article XLIX Artificial Intelligence
rules.applies_when: a producer signatory to the IATSE Basic Agreement (Hollywood West Coast studio locals) assigns or allows AI systems in covered crew work, or asks to scan a crew member's visual or vocal likeness
requires: Crew assigned to use AI systems (including prompting or overseeing them) stay covered by the agreement while doing so.
Do not require an employee to provide prompts in a way that displaces a covered employee.

Employees using AI must follow the producer's written AI policies (ethics, privacy, security, copyrightability); the producer may require prior consent for AI use and may reject AI use or output, and must give those policies to the union.
If the producer requires AI use, consult the employee on request where production time allows.
Negotiate reasonable reimbursement if the producer uses an employee's own AI system.

Indemnify employees against claims from AI use or output within the scope of employment, unless gross negligence, willful misconduct or breach of disclosed policies, and provided the employee disclosed the AI use.

Do not scan an employee's visual or vocal likeness without clear, conspicuous, separately signed consent with a reasonably specific use description; consent cannot be a condition of employment, and the form must be given to the union first.
Meet the union semi-annually (industry-wide) and quarterly (company by company) on request about AI use; negotiate over the impact of AI on bargaining-unit employees on request.
evidence: Copy of the producer's written AI-use policy as given to crew and to the union
Per-shot record of which crew member used which AI system, and the producer's consent where required
Record that the employee disclosed AI use (needed to keep indemnity)
Signed scan-consent form for any crew likeness capture, stating consent is not a condition of employment
Consultation requests and responses where AI use was required
workflow_signals: generative nodes run by union crew on covered productions
employee-owned models, LoRAs or API keys used on production work
photogrammetry or voice capture of crew members (e.g. stand-ins, stunt or crowd reference)

The MOA copy is hosted by Deadline, not IATSE. Article XLIX applies prospectively from the later of 2024-08-04 or the first Sunday after AMPTP receives notice of ratification. Producers keep the right to use AI, including on creative elements; existing 'traditional AI' (CGI, VFX) practices continue. Arbitrators cannot prohibit or restrict AI use. Covers West Coast studio locals; it does not cover non-union VFX houses, and Canadian IATSE locals (e.g. Local 891 Vancouver, AQTIS 514 Montreal) have their own agreements, not checked. rules.authority: The Animation Guild (IATSE Local 839) / AMPTP
rules.title: 2024 Animation Guild Agreement: Article 21.N Artificial Intelligence
rules.applies_when: a signatory animation producer asks or requires TAG-covered artists, writers or technical staff to use generative AI, provides AI-generated written material to an animation writer, or asks to scan an employee's likeness
requires: Give advance written notice to any employee who might be asked or required to use a generative AI system in covered work.

corrections: The EU does not legally require proof that a human was in the loop for an AI-generated shot. AI Act Art. 14 (human oversight) applies only to high-risk AI systems (Annex I products and Annex III areas such as biometrics, employment, education, law enforcement and justice). Creative content generation is not in Annex III, and Annex III obligations are now deferred to 2027-12-02. What applies to creative work is Art. 50 transparency: providers mark output in machine-readable form, and deployers disclose deepfakes (lighter duty for evidently artistic or fictional works). Art. 50's human-review/editorial-responsibility exemption covers only AI-generated text on matters of public interest, not images or video. The Commission's Art. 50 guidelines (C(2026) 5054, 2026-07-20) add that AI backgrounds, special effects and standard post-processing in film are unlikely to be deepfakes, while digital replicas, de-aging and synthetic performers are likely deepfakes that, in a film, fall under the lighter disclosure for evidently artistic or fictional works.

Human involvement matters in the EU and elsewhere for copyright protectability, not for legality. Under the CJEU originality test (free and creative choices), the Czech 10 C 13/2023 ruling (2023-10-11; the claim failed because the claimant could not prove he wrote the prompt, so its copyrightability statements are obiter) and the AG Munich February 2026 logos ruling, little or no human creative input means no copyright. Records of human creative choices are therefore valuable evidence, but they are not a regulatory compliance requirement.

In US film and TV, the closest thing to a 'human in the loop' duty is contractual: DGA terms (AI is not a person; consult the director, and under the 2026 deal AI footage falls under the director's creative control), SAG-AFTRA consent rules, and the Academy's 99th Oscars rules, under which generative AI neither helps nor harms eligibility and voters weigh how much of the creative authorship was human. The US Copyright Office registration guidance requires disclosing AI material and describing the human contribution.

MPAA was renamed the Motion Picture Association (MPA) on 2019-09-18. The MPA has no rules on creative use of AI, copyright clearance or disclosure. The MPA does publish binding-in-practice AI rules for vendors, but as content security, not creative or legal clearance. The MPA Content Security Best Practices v5.3.2 with AI Supplemental v1.0 (TPN, 2026-09-23) require client approval for AI tools on client content, an approved-AI inventory, per-project approval records, AI audit logs (prompts, outputs, identity, timestamps), model scanning and segmented import, no training on client content without written consent, and human approval of agentic actions.
The DGA terms require consultation with, and (from 2026) director control over AI footage. No public source says director sign-off on each AI shot is contractually required.

California AI Transparency Act: since SB 1000 (signed 2026-09-30) there is no 1-million-user threshold, no manifest-disclosure option, and the film/TV/streaming exclusion is gone (only non-user-generated video games are excluded).

EU AI Act Art. 50(2) marking falls on providers of generative systems (model and tool vendors), not on every studio that uses them. A studio that builds or substantially modifies its own generative system may become a provider. Systems already on the market before 2026-08-02 have until 2026-12-02 under the Digital Omnibus (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744). Deployer deepfake disclosure under Art. 50(4) applied from 2026-08-02 without delay. Per the Commission guidelines, intermediate outputs used only inside closed-loop film, animation, games or advertising production need no marking; only final outputs do.

The EU Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content (final 2026-06-10) is voluntary and, per IPTC, does not name C2PA. It calls for signed, time-stamped metadata plus watermarking under 'relevant standards'. The Commission and AI Board have since assessed it as adequate, and the deployer icon can be the plain 'AI' acronym.

Thaler v. Perlmutter settles only that an AI cannot be the author when there is no human contribution. It does not set how much human input is enough; that question is open (Allen v. Perlmutter was still pending when last checked).

The NO FAKES Act is not law (reintroduced 2026-05-20; reported out of Senate Judiciary in June 2026; a unanimous-consent attempt was blocked on 2026-09-30). The TAKE IT DOWN Act is in force but limited to nonconsensual intimate imagery.

US Copyright Office Part 2 says AI used as an assistive tool (e.g. de-aging, color correction, crowd removal) does not undermine protection. Routine VFX uses of AI are treated differently from prompt-only generation, as are SAG-AFTRA's exempt post-production alterations.

Under the Commission's Art. 50 guidelines, most VFX uses of AI in a film are not deepfakes: AI backgrounds, set extensions, special effects and standard pre/post-processing are 'not likely' to make content falsely appear authentic. AI actors, digital replicas of real or deceased actors, de-aging and simulated performances are likely deepfakes. In a film shown in cinemas or on streaming they qualify for the lighter disclosure, which still requires some disclosure.

A studio does not need to machine-mark every intermediate AI render. The guidelines exclude outputs used only inside closed-loop film, animation, games or advertising production; only the final output must be marked, and that duty is the provider's.

A non-EU studio is a deployer under Art. 50(4) when it directs or authorises distribution of the content in the EU, including posting it on the open internet. A client that commissions work without controlling the AI use is not the deployer; the vendor that decides is.
The deployer's deepfake disclosure cannot rely on the provider's invisible watermark or C2PA metadata. It must be perceivable without tools (visible or audible).

Art. 53 training-data summaries and copyright policies are duties of the model provider, not of the studio using the model. Open-weight models released under a free and open-source licence are exempt from documentation duties but must still publish the training-data summary and keep a copyright policy.

Italy's AI Law (Law 132/2025) did not create a mandatory 'IA' label for films or TV. Its creative-sector provisions are the human-authorship amendment to copyright law, a TDM rule, and a new crime of harmful non-consensual AI deepfake dissemination (Art. 612-quater Penal Code).
Denmark's 'copyright in your own face' law is not yet in force: bill L 49 was tabled on 2026-10-08 with a target of 2027-01-01, after an earlier version lapsed.
From 2026-12-02 the AI Act bans using AI to generate realistic intimate or sexual imagery of an identifiable person without explicit consent. Consented intimate-scene VFX is not covered by the ban.

An 'air-gapped content network' is one of two accepted options under MPA/TPN TS-2.5: a Layer 1 physical air gap or logical VLAN segmentation, with no dual-homed bridging. v5.3.2 requires pre-trained LLMs to be imported into a 'segmented and restricted network' before use. It no longer recommends using only internally managed, sandboxed LLMs.

C2PA 2.4 (April 2026) is out and adds a c2pa.ai-disclosure assertion with a humanOversightLevel field (fully_autonomous / prompt_guided / human_validated). C2PA now offers a standard way to state human involvement, though the field is optional and self-declared.

For VFX composites, IPTC's guide separates three cases. GenAI editing of a camera plate (inpaint, outpaint, GenAI effects on footage) is compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia. A comp of live action plus separately generated elements is compositeSynthetic. A fully generated shot, including a deepfake that blends a real actor with a trained model, is trainedAlgorithmicMedia. Non-generative AI fixes such as denoise or sharpen are algorithmicallyEnhanced, not GenAI.

Netflix's guidance does not ban GenAI in final deliverables outright. Coverage describes final-deliverable use, talent likeness, personal or Netflix data, third-party IP and key story elements as triggers for escalation and possible written approval, and notifying the Netflix contact is expected for all GenAI use.
The UK has no blanket AI-label rule for ads. CAP/BCAP require disclosure only where omission would mislead, and a label does not cure a misleading AI depiction.

Meta's political/social-issue ad policy now (from 2026-06-01) adds automated detection of third-party GenAI media on top of advertiser self-disclosure. The earlier policy URL with a lowercase path returns 404.
New York's post-mortem digital replica law is S.8391/A.8882 (Chapter 616 of 2025), not S.8882.

California now has its own synthetic-performer ad disclosure law (SB 1050, operative 2027-01-01). It is broader than New York's: it covers audio-only ads, has no knowledge requirement and allows private enforcement.
Illinois' film/TV portrayal exemption does not cover the digital-replica distribution rule; replica uses in fiction need consent unless a narrower s35(c) exemption applies.
Korea's AI Basic Act labelling duty falls on AI business operators; on Shin & Kim's reading of MSIT guidance, a film producer that only uses AI-generated CG is generally a user, not an operator.

Japan's Art. 30-4 does not cover a LoRA or fine-tune built to reproduce a specific creator's expression, and reliance on a work is generally presumed if it was in the model's training data, even if the user did not know.

The 2023 SAG-AFTRA rules are no longer the operative contract: the 2023 TV/Theatrical Agreement expired 2026-06-30 and the 2026 agreement (ratified 2026-06-04) applies from 2026-07-01. It keeps the 2023 framework and amends it.

A replica made from the picture's own footage, with no scan session, is still an employment-based replica under the 2026 SAG-AFTRA terms. Training an identity model on dailies does not avoid the consent rules.
Under SAG-AFTRA terms, foreign-language dubbing with a replica did not need consent under the 2023 rules; consent is needed only for pictures starting principal photography on or after 2027-07-01.

The 2026 SAG-AFTRA, WGA and (reportedly) DGA training-data terms require notice to the union and a meeting, not consent or payment, and apply only to compensated licenses to non-affiliated third parties for public-facing commercial generative AI systems.
SAG-AFTRA's 2026 'Synthetic' rule does not ban synthetic performers; it requires notice, bargaining and a 'significant additional value' showing, enforceable through arbitration.

The 99th Oscars rules do not require human authorship as a threshold for films using generative AI; AI 'neither helps nor harms', and voters weigh the degree of human authorship. Human-performed acting with consent, and human-authored screenplays, are the hard eligibility conditions.
IATSE and Animation Guild contracts let producers require AI use; crew protections are notice (TAG), consultation, non-displacement by prompting, indemnity and scan consent, not a right to refuse AI.

Getty v Stability (UK) did not decide that AI training is lawful in the UK. Getty dropped its training claim because training took place outside the UK. Only the secondary-infringement theory about importing the model weights was decided, and that is on appeal.
Getty's US case was not transferred. Getty voluntarily dismissed the Delaware action and refiled in N.D. Cal. on 2025-08-14.
The CMS case tracker says Stability was granted leave to appeal on secondary infringement. IPKat and Taylor Wessing report that permission went to Getty, which lost on that point.
Some blogs say the Andersen v. Stability AI jury trial began in September 2026. Docket-based trackers show summary judgment set for February 2027 and no trial date.
USCO Part 3 is still a pre-publication report, even though some commentary calls it 'final'.

The removal of the Register of Copyrights has not taken effect. Perlmutter remains in office under a D.C. Circuit injunction, and the Supreme Court denied a stay on 2026-06-30 without ruling on the merits.

Bartz v. Anthropic did not hold that AI training is fair use in general. A district-court order found training on lawfully acquired books to be fair use and pirated library copies not to be, and the settlement does not release claims about outputs.
Kadrey v. Meta did not hold that training Llama was lawful. The judge said the ruling reflects these plaintiffs' failure to build a record of market harm.
Thomson Reuters v. ROSS (3d Cir. 2026) concerns non-generative AI, and the court distinguished generative-AI training cases.
Chinese law on AI image copyright is not uniformly permissive. Li v Liu (2023) and Changshu (2025) granted protection; Zhangjiagang (2025) refused it for lack of documented human input.

interop.movielabs: MovieLabs has not published an AI provenance spec or an AI extension to the Ontology for Media Creation (OMC). Its 2026-07-08 post 'Building Foundations for Trusted and Reliable AI in Media Creation Workflows' (Rich Berger) lists 'Transparency & Provenance' as an AI focus area: capturing asset lineage and creative contributions, both human and AI. It names no schema, fields or repos and says MovieLabs is not a policymaking body. That work runs through the MovieLabs Industry Forum's AI Implementation Group. The current OMC-JSON schema (v2.8, MovieLabs/OMC repo, last pushed 2026-02-07) already has a generic Provenance utility: CreatedBy (a Participant, which can be a Person, Organization, Department or Service), createdOn, Role, Origin (an Asset), reason and annotation. v2.6-2.8 added omc:Software. MovieLabs' omc-util repo carries v3.0 templates, including Provenance, but OMC v3.0 publication was not verified. omc-data-pipeline, which emits OMC-JSON v3.0 bundles with a provenance.json per file, was archived 2026-10-06 and moved into 'Labkoat-API'. A ComfyAudit export that maps each run to OMC Asset plus Provenance (CreatedBy = a Service participant for the model/tool, Origin = input plates or assets, Role, createdOn), plus a C2PA manifest, is the closest available interoperability path.
interop.etc_comfy_node: No ETC@USC + MovieLabs ComfyUI node that records generative provenance was found. The only MovieLabs ComfyUI repo is MovieLabs/comfyui-movielabs-util (https://github.com/MovieLabs/comfyui-movielabs-util): description 'ComfyUI Custom Nodes', created 2025-03-18, last push 2025-07-12, no license file, Python. It provides two nodes. PublishAsset publishes an output (original plus optional proxy) to the filesystem and to ShotGrid as a new Version, with artist login, shot code, task, notes, automatic version numbering and naming checks, and EXR sequence checks. PublishBlender versions a .blend file. Its config.json points at an 'etc-europa' ShotGrid site and an output path segment 'PATHWAYS', with tasks Generate Image, Generate Video, Generate Blender Ref, CG Relight, Camera Tracking, Slap Comp, Comp and Upres. This suggests, but does not confirm, that it was built for ETC's hybrid AI/live-action short 'Pathways' (dir. Felipe Vargas). It does not capture prompts, models, seeds, LoRAs or C2PA. Its provenance value is tracking who published which version, for which shot and task, in ShotGrid. Two open issues (2025-10-22) propose a pyproject.toml and a Comfy Registry publishing action. For interop, ComfyAudit could read or write the same ShotGrid Version (shot code, task, version number, artist) and attach its provenance record to it. Related third-party packs (seen in search results only, not fetched): ksallee/sg-comfyui (records a generation as a Flow/ShotGrid Version with generation details) and mdietrich/comfyui_MDPack (provenance-aware save node with IPTC/XMP AI disclosure and optional C2PA signing). SMPTE launched a Content Provenance and Authenticity in Media study group in July 2025 (search result only).

research.statement: These rules were researched and re-checked on 2026-10-15 by an AI model (Claude, by Anthropic) using live web research, not by a lawyer. The model's own training knowledge ends in June 2026, so anything after that rests only on the sources cited. Each rule records what its check rests on: the primary text itself, an official summary, law-firm or press reports, or search results only, plus the date of each source. The SAG-AFTRA 2026 terms come from the union's official summary of the tentative agreement (2026-05-11), supplied by Doug Hogan. Four high-impact findings were re-read against their sources by the coordinating model: the Commission's Art. 50 guidelines, the MPA/TPN AI controls, Disney v. MiniMax and California SB 1000. Several official sites blocked automated reading, and those rules say so. Full union contract texts and some statutes were not available. Treat this as research to take to counsel, not legal advice.
research.method: Five parallel research passes (unions and guilds; copyright and AI litigation; EU and member states; US states and Asia-Pacific; industry, platforms, insurance and standards). Every existing rule was re-checked and its verdict recorded (confirmed, corrected or could-not-verify); new rules are marked new.
research.previous_pass: The first version of this file was also dated 2026-10-15; how it was researched was not recorded.

facts.third-party-characters: The shot's prompts, references or outputs depict or evoke characters, franchises or other IP owned by someone other than the studio or its client.
facts.model-stable-diffusion: A Stable Diffusion-family checkpoint was used in the shot (SD 1.x/2.x/SDXL/SD3, or a community fine-tune derived from one).
facts.model-midjourney: Midjourney (image or video) was used in the shot.
facts.model-minimax: A MiniMax / Hailuo model was used in the shot, via API, partner node or local weights.
facts.client-netflix: Netflix is the client or commissioner of the work (a Netflix original, or a vendor contract under a Netflix production).
facts.tpn-vendor: The studio is a TPN-assessed service provider, or handles pre-release content for an MPA member studio (Netflix, Paramount, Amazon, Sony Pictures, Universal, Disney, Warner Bros.) under content-security terms.
facts.eo-insurance: The production carries, or must obtain, media/production errors & omissions insurance covering the delivered work.
facts.union-crew: The shot was worked on by crew covered by a union crew agreement (e.g. IATSE Basic Agreement, Animation Guild), so AI-use notice, consultation, policy and scanning rules for crew apply.
facts.animation: The shot belongs to an animated production (or animation department), which brings in Animation Guild and animation-performer terms.
facts.ai-music: The shot or deliverable includes music or sound generated by an AI audio/music model.
facts.copyright-claim: The studio or client intends to register or enforce copyright in the shot.
